prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty.

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I keep B001 first. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice idea is a concrete, original conception, and Ye's group carried it to the best measured uncertainties and to clock-comparison and many-body clock physics. The result is a clean measurement advance of about two orders of magnitude over the caesium standard, with independent confirmation at several national laboratories and in more than one species. It is relevant beyond timekeeping: tests of the constancy of constants, dark-sector searches, relativistic geodesy and the planned redefinition of the second. Four members placed it first and two more placed it second or third, which at least indicates that the attribution (two names, one concept and one record-setting realisation) is not controversial inside this committee. Among the shortlisted candidates it is the only one where credit maps onto two named people without leaving out a decisive contributor in the credited list.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. Hall and Hansch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland (2012, quantum control of ions, which also underlies the best ion clocks) already honoured adjacent parts of precision spectroscopy, and some will see this as a third chapter in one story. A second reservation is that this is a measurement and metrology achievement whose most dramatic payoffs (a redefined second, a detected variation of constants, a dark-matter signal) have not yet arrived. Finally, others who built the clocks (for example Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley) are outside the credited names, and Ye's relation to the comb prize is something the citation must handle carefully.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos (B027, Halzen alone) first, as a new observational window with a clear discovery character, while acknowledging that a single-name credit is thin.
responses.response: I agree that opening a new window is the kind of discovery the prize is meant for, and the diffuse flux is firmly established. My difficulty is the attribution. A one-name configuration for a project of this scale would draw immediate objections, and the pioneers of the detection concept and of the instrument are not available among the credited names. I also note that the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are still at moderate significance, so the interpretation is younger than the clocks. I would keep B027 as a serious candidate for a later year when a fuller configuration can be justified, but I do not think it can carry this year's prize.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B017) first as a prediction followed by an experiment that opened moire quantum matter, but names unresolved credit to Cao, Dean, Young, Yacoby and Efetov and an unsettled pairing mechanism.
responses.response: I share the scientific admiration, and I ranked B017 third myself. The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction paired with the 2018 experiment is a rare case of a theory-experiment sequence creating a field. Where I differ is on timing and attribution: you also note that the pairing mechanism is not settled and that experimental credit extends beyond the lead group, and I would add that the first author of the decisive experiment is not among the credited names. Eight years is short compared with the lattice clocks, whose 10^-18 performance has been reproduced by independent laboratories. I would put B017 as the first alternative, and I think it is a stronger case in a few years if the mechanism question becomes clearer.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B001 first for the same reasons of control of atomic structure turned into a new measurement capability, and places the Higgs experimental discovery (B002) second, noting that the credited names are detector leaders rather than individual analysts.
responses.response: We agree on B001, and I accept her point that the 2005 comb prize is complementary rather than overlapping, which answers part of my own novelty worry. On B002 I stay more cautious than she does. The importance of the discovery is beyond doubt, but the credited three are conceivers and builders of the experiments, and awarding detector leadership instead of the discovery itself raises an attribution precedent that the committee has so far avoided; I ranked it fifth. I would not exclude it, but I do not see it as more robust than the clocks.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B001 first as a clean instrument-driven discovery or invention with concrete, measurable impact, and B017 second, while noting that attribution in B015 (tunnel magnetoresistance) and B010 is only partly resolved.
responses.response: I agree that B001 fits a prize for a specific invention with a measurable result. I would qualify her high placement of B015: the TMR credit between Miyazaki and Moodera in 1995 and Parkin and the Yuasa group in 2004, plus the coherent-tunnelling theory, is not resolved by the three credited names, and it follows the 2007 GMR prize. On B010 I come to the same conclusion as she does on attribution, namely that the Kane, Mele, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Molenkamp and Hasan allocation is too unstable for a prize this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the 2005 (combs) and 2012 (ion quantum control) prizes as already covering the clock theme, so that a lattice-clock prize looks like a repeat.
How the citation should balance Katori's concept against the experimental precision race and whether Ye's record is best described as realisation or as co-invention.
Whether contributors outside the credited names (for example Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley) can be set aside without unfairness, which cannot be tested from the shortlist alone.
My knowledge of the detailed history is recalled from memory rather than verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I have no documented connection to Katori or Ye, and the documented co-authors and institutions do not overlap with the B001 candidates; my statistical-physics background gives me no direct stake in the clock field.
